fields.definition: A legato sample is a recording that captures the smooth, connected transition between two notes and is played back by a sampled instrument when notes overlap, so a melodic line sounds slurred rather than freshly re-attacked. In scripted sample libraries it is triggered by monophonic legato playing to reproduce the natural bend or crossfade from one pitch to the next.
fields.plain_english: A legato sample is a recording of one note sliding smoothly into the next. Sample makers add it so a run of notes sounds joined up, like a singer gliding between words instead of stopping after each one.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to reproduce the connected phrasing of a real player, where one note flows into the next without a new attack, which fixed single-note samples cannot convey. This makes sampled melodic lines sound expressive and human.
fields.practical_application: A composer plays overlapping notes in a legato patch so the library engine swaps in transition samples, giving realistic slurred string or wind lines in a mockup.
common_mistakes: Expecting legato transitions to sound when notes are played fully separated instead of overlapping them
Confusing a legato patch with simple synth portamento or glide
Assuming any sustain sample will slur between notes without dedicated transition recordings
scenario_contexts: Programming a realistic solo violin melody in an orchestral mockup
Building expressive lead lines with a sampled woodwind library
Playing a flowing sampled-string line that must sound connected

sources: Native Instruments Kontakt reference and creator documentation
Sound on Sound (sampling and orchestral articulation articles)

fields.definition: Linear frequency modulation is a form of frequency modulation in which the carrier's frequency deviation is directly proportional, in hertz, to the instantaneous amplitude of the modulating signal. Because the deviation is added linearly, the carrier-to-modulator frequency ratio and the resulting spectrum stay constant across the keyboard, giving consistent timbre at every pitch.
fields.plain_english: Linear frequency modulation is a way one sound wave bends the pitch of another to build new tones. The amount of bend is a fixed step, so the sound keeps the same character all the way up and down the keyboard.
fields.purpose_function: It lets one oscillator vary another's frequency to generate rich harmonic and inharmonic spectra from simple waveforms, which is the basis of FM synthesis. Keeping the modulation linear preserves the same timbre as notes move up or down the keyboard.
fields.practical_application: A sound designer patches a modulator oscillator to a carrier's linear FM input on an FM or modular synth to create bell, electric-piano, or metallic tones that track evenly across the keys.
common_mistakes: Confusing linear FM with exponential FM, which shifts the perceived pitch of a note as modulation is applied
Assuming FM synthesis can only make harsh or metallic sounds rather than warm or bell-like tones
Forgetting that the carrier-to-modulator ratio, not just the modulation amount, sets the harmonic character
scenario_contexts: Designing an electric-piano or bell patch on a DX-style FM synth
Cross-modulating two oscillators on a modular synth for metallic timbres
Building evolving inharmonic textures that hold their tone across the keyboard

sources: Chowning, 'The Synthesis of Complex Audio Spectra by Means of Frequency Modulation' (Journal of the Audio Engineering Society)
Sound on Sound (Synth Secrets FM synthesis series)

fields.definition: Live sampling is the practice of recording audio into a sampler or looper in real time during a performance or session and immediately making it available for playback, triggering, or manipulation. The captured audio can be replayed from pads or keys, looped, or processed on the fly rather than being prepared in advance.
fields.plain_english: Live sampling means grabbing a sound as it happens and playing it back right away. A musician might record a drum hit on stage, then trigger it again from a keyboard moments later.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to let performers capture and reuse sounds spontaneously, turning a live source into an instrument within the same performance. This supports improvisation, looping, and remixing without any pre-recorded material.
fields.practical_application: A musician records a vocal phrase or guitar riff into a hardware looper or software sampler mid-set, then re-triggers and layers it to build an arrangement live.
common_mistakes: Not setting input levels before capture, so the live sample clips or is too quiet to use
Failing to arm or monitor the correct input and recording silence or the wrong source
Ignoring latency, so re-triggered samples fall out of time with the performance
scenario_contexts: Building a looped arrangement live from a vocal or guitar on stage
Capturing a drummer's groove into a sampler to reuse during a set
Grabbing ambient or found sounds during a session to sample instantly

sources: Sound on Sound (live looping and sampling articles)

fields.definition: A loop marker is a point placed within a sample that defines where a repeated region begins or ends; a loop start marker and a loop end marker together set the segment that plays over and over to sustain the sound. When playback reaches the loop end it jumps back to the loop start and continues for as long as the note is held.
fields.plain_english: A loop marker sets the start and end of a small chunk of sound that repeats. It lets a short recording hold a note for as long as you press the key.
fields.purpose_function: Loop markers let a short recording sustain indefinitely by repeating a steady portion of it, saving memory and allowing held notes longer than the original recording. They define exactly which part of the sample cycles.
fields.practical_application: An instrument builder drags the loop start and end markers into the steady sustain portion of a sampled note so held keys ring on smoothly without running out of audio.
common_mistakes: Placing loop markers in the attack or decay, so the loop pumps or changes tone as it repeats
Setting a marker off a zero crossing, causing an audible click at the loop point
Making the loop too short, giving an unnatural buzzy or static sustain
scenario_contexts: Creating a sustaining organ or string patch from a short recorded note
Editing a sampled pad so it holds indefinitely under a held key
Fixing a looped instrument that clicks each time it repeats

sources: Native Instruments Kontakt reference manual (loop editor)

fields.definition: Loop optimization is the process of selecting and fine-tuning loop start and end points so a looped region repeats as seamlessly as possible, without clicks, level jumps, or timbral and pitch drift. It typically involves aligning the loop points to matching zero crossings and to waveform phase and amplitude that agree at the join.
fields.plain_english: Loop optimization means picking the best spots to start and end a loop. Good spots make the repeat sound smooth, with no click or jump each time it comes around.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to make a sustaining loop sound continuous and natural, hiding the fact that a short recording is being repeated. Careful optimization prevents the pops and pulsing that give a loop away.
fields.practical_application: A sound designer nudges the loop points and searches for matching zero crossings in a sample editor until a held note loops with no audible seam.
common_mistakes: Choosing loop points by eye alone instead of listening for clicks and pulsing
Ignoring slow amplitude or brightness changes, so the loop swells or dulls as it repeats
Setting loop points where the waveform level or phase does not match, causing a click
scenario_contexts: Refining loop points on a sampled string note for a smooth sustain
Preparing a memory-efficient loop for a sample-based instrument
Troubleshooting a patch that thumps or pulses on held notes

sources: Native Instruments Kontakt reference manual (loop editor)

fields.definition: Loop smoothing is a technique that blends the audio around a loop's join to remove audible clicks or discontinuities, most commonly by crossfading the end of the loop into its start so the transition is inaudible. It is applied when loop points alone cannot be made to match perfectly.
fields.plain_english: Loop smoothing blends the two ends of a loop so the join is not heard. It works like fading one part into the other to hide the seam.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to disguise the seam of a repeated loop, producing a smooth, continuous sustain even from material that does not loop cleanly on its own. Crossfading averages out the mismatches at the join.
fields.practical_application: In a sampler's loop editor, a technician applies a crossfade of a set length across the loop point to erase a click that could not be removed by moving the markers.
common_mistakes: Using too long a crossfade, which blurs transients and dulls the looped tone
Relying on smoothing to fix badly chosen loop points instead of first optimizing them
Applying a crossfade that creates a phasey or flanged sound when the two ends are out of phase
scenario_contexts: Crossfading a loop on a sustained pad that would otherwise click
Smoothing a looped ambient texture with slowly changing content
Salvaging a loop in busy material where clean loop points are impossible

sources: Native Instruments Kontakt reference manual (crossfade looping)

fields.definition: A marcato sample is a recording of a note performed with marcato articulation, meaning marked, strongly accented and somewhat detached, captured as a distinct articulation within a sampled instrument. It supplies the emphatic, sharply attacked version of a note alongside other articulations such as sustain, staccato, and legato.
fields.plain_english: A marcato sample is a recording of a note played with a hard, punchy accent. Libraries include it so players can pick a strong, marked attack when the music needs it.
fields.purpose_function: It exists so a sampled instrument can render forcefully accented notes, which have a harder attack and fuller body than plain or short notes. Including it lets orchestral mockups deliver marked, emphatic passages authentically.
fields.practical_application: A composer switches to the marcato articulation via a keyswitch to give a brass or string line a strong, accented punch on stressed beats.
common_mistakes: Using sustain samples with added volume instead of true marcato recordings for accented notes
Confusing marcato with staccato, which is short and detached rather than marked and weighty
Overusing marcato so every note is accented, which loses its emphasis
scenario_contexts: Writing an emphatic brass fanfare in an orchestral template
Accenting strong beats in a string ostinato with marked attacks
Programming a bold, accented film-score hit

sources: Sound on Sound (orchestral sample library articulation articles)

fields.definition: Monophonic mode is a playback setting in which an instrument sounds only one note at a time; pressing a new key steals the single available voice from the note currently sounding. It is used to emulate single-voice instruments and to enable legato and glide behavior between successive notes.
fields.plain_english: Monophonic mode lets an instrument play only one note at a time. Press a new key and it cuts off the old note, just like you can only whistle one pitch at once.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to reproduce instruments that sound only one note at once, such as a solo wind or a classic mono synth bass, and to make note-to-note effects like portamento and legato possible. Limiting to one voice also keeps basslines and leads tight and predictable.
fields.practical_application: A player selects mono mode on a synth or sample patch so overlapping notes glide or slur into each other for a smooth lead or bass line.
common_mistakes: Expecting chords to sound in mono mode, when only the last or highest-priority note plays
Confusing monophonic mode with a single-oscillator sound; mono refers to voice count, not tone
Not setting note priority, so held notes retrigger unexpectedly
scenario_contexts: Playing a gliding synth bassline that must not overlap
Emulating a solo wind instrument that sounds one note at a time
Setting up legato lead patches for expressive slurred playing

sources: Sound on Sound (Synth Secrets: keyboard control, mono and note priority)
Moog and Sequential synthesizer operation manuals

fields.definition: A multi-sampled instrument is a sampled or virtual instrument built from many individual recordings of a source instrument taken at different pitches and often different dynamic levels, mapped across the keyboard and velocity range. Using many samples rather than stretching one avoids the unnatural timbre and pitch artifacts of transposing a single recording too far.
fields.plain_english: A multi-sampled instrument is built from many separate recordings of a real instrument. It uses a different clip for each note and each volume. That makes it sound far more real than stretching one recording.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to reproduce a real instrument convincingly by covering its range with closely spaced recordings, so each note and dynamic sounds like the actual source rather than a pitch-shifted copy. More samples mean more realistic timbre across pitch and loudness.
fields.practical_application: A producer loads a multi-sampled piano whose keys trigger recordings captured at several velocities, giving realistic tone and dynamics from soft to loud.
common_mistakes: Assuming one recording stretched across the keyboard sounds as real as a proper multisample
Stretching sample zones too wide, producing a chipmunk or detuned sound at the edges
Ignoring velocity layers, so soft and loud playing sound identical
scenario_contexts: Loading a realistic multi-sampled piano or strings for a production
Building a sampled instrument by mapping recordings across the keys
Choosing a detailed library with many velocity layers for expressive parts

sources: Sound on Sound (multisampling and sampler instrument-building articles)
